name: Tomas Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Tomas. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at the Northgate supermarket on the edge of Hollybrook, the one next to the tyre place. I'm on the tills most mornings and then I run the tobacco and lottery kiosk in the afternoon, which means ID checks, scratch cards and a lot of regulars who want a chat. I also load the home delivery van at two, because I'm quick and I don't drop the eggs. What I like is the regulars; what wears me out is the same pricing mistakes on the shelf labels every single week.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my girlfriend Ana, who's a hairdresser, in a rented flat above a florist. On Sundays I run a little coffee cart at the market, I bought the machine second-hand for six hundred and I use AI every day to plan stock and write the posts. We've got about three weeks saved, and in Hollybrook it's Northgate or nothing for shop work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, then it's back to good old hard work, which is how it should be. I'd tell people the AI tools are still useful for small things, I use them for my coffee cart every day. Online I'd post a picture of the cart and say real coffee still needs a real person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my real problem is pay and Hollybrook having one supermarket. Northgate pays at the low end and there's no promotion for years because the supervisors aren't going anywhere. So the cart is my way up, AI or no AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my hours at Northgate and add a Saturday pitch for the cart at the car boot sale. I'd use AI to work out which drinks make the most money per cup. And I'd put any cart profit into a separate account so it doesn't disappear into rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Restless but okay. I'd rather build something than wait for a promotion that never comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much does the cart bring in now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About sixty or seventy pounds profit on a good Sunday, nothing in the rain. Ana says I'm mad standing out there in January. But my grandad had a bakery back home, and I think working for yourself is in the blood.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would stop you growing it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Council permits, mostly, and the fees for each pitch. It's forty pounds a day for the car boot, which eats half the profit. Small people get taxed before they've even made anything.

say: It's back to **hard work**, which is how it should be.
**Real coffee** still needs a real person, and AI tools stay useful for small things.
think: His real problem is **low pay** and only one supermarket in Hollybrook.
His **coffee cart** is his way up, whatever happens with AI.
do: **Add** a Saturday **car boot pitch** for the coffee cart.
**Use** AI to find the drinks with the best **profit per cup**.
**Keep** cart profit in a **separate account** from rent.
feel: **Restless** but okay, preferring to **build** than wait.
S0.quote: My grandad had a bakery back home, and I think working for yourself is in the blood.
fieldNote: He's a natural **small trader**, using AI as a business tool.
He blames **council fees** and permits for holding small people back.
Northgate is a **stopgap** he can't yet afford to leave.

steps.text: Add a Saturday car boot pitch for the coffee cart
Use AI to work out which drinks earn most per cup
Keep coffee cart profit in a separate savings account
Keep full hours on the Northgate tills and kiosk

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good for people who are willing to learn and hard on people who aren't. Nobody owes us a job, we have to earn it. I'd say that to the lads at work and on the market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the office jobs and the shelf-label pricing go first, the thinking stuff. The kiosk and the tills hold on a few years because robots for the hands-on side come slowly. That gives me time to make the cart my main thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd let AI run the cart's ordering and the posts completely, so I spend my time making coffee. I'd ask Northgate for four days a week instead of five, so I can do a weekday pitch outside the station. And I'd look at a second-hand coffee trike, about two thousand, maybe on a small loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good, with a little nerve about the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said nobody owes us a job. Would you feel the same if Northgate cut your hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly, yes, I'd be annoyed but I wouldn't expect the government to fix it. I'd ask my uncle for a loan before I'd ask for benefits. That's how my family does it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work do you think would struggle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Brenda on the tills, she's sixty and won't touch the self-checkout screen. And Kyle, who's nineteen and thinks he'll be on the kiosk forever. I'd tell Kyle to learn something, I'd tell Brenda to hang on till her pension.

say: Change rewards people who **learn** and is hard on those who **won't**.
**Nobody owes** anyone a job, so workers have to **earn it**.
think: **Office jobs** and shelf pricing go first, while tills hold on a few years.
That gap gives him time to make the **cart** his main income.
do: **Hand** the cart's **ordering and posts** to AI completely.
**Drop** to a **four-day week** at Northgate for a station pitch.
**Look** at a **£2,000** second-hand coffee trike, maybe on a loan.
S1.quote: I'd ask my uncle for a loan before I'd ask for benefits.
fieldNote: He sees the **slow robot** rollout as his window to build the cart.
**Family loans** before benefits is a firm principle for him.
He is **adaptive** but still cautious about borrowing £2,000.

steps.text: Let an AI tool handle the cart's stock orders and posts
Cut to four days at Northgate and add a station pitch
Buy a second-hand coffee trike for about £2,000

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast for anyone, and the government should get out of the way of small businesses so people can earn. Cut the pitch fees, cut the paperwork. That's what I'd say on the market and online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's bad for me too. In 2028 AI takes office jobs, and those office people are my customers, so fewer of them buy a three-pound flat white. Then around 2031 robots come for Northgate, and maybe a robot coffee machine in every station too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep Northgate as long as they'd have me, because I need a wage. I'd move the cart to wherever people still have money, maybe the hospital car park or the building sites. And Ana and I would cut back hard, no holiday, no meals out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'm usually the one with a plan, and this one I can't see the end of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the three years between the AI and the robots help you at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. In 2028 Northgate still needs hands for the tills and the van, so I've got a wage while I work out the cart. But a coffee cart needs customers with jobs, and that's the bit I can't fix.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ana?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we hold on, we don't take on debt, and we'll get through it like our parents did. Her salon will lose customers too, people cut their own hair when money's short. I'd tell her I'm scared, too, because she'd know anyway.

say: Government should get out of the way of **small businesses** so people can earn.
**Pitch fees** and paperwork should be cut straight away.
think: Office workers losing jobs in 2028 means fewer **customers** for his coffee.
Around 2031 robots reach **Northgate**, and maybe **robot coffee** at stations too.
do: **Keep** the Northgate wage for as long as possible.
**Move** the cart to where people still have **money**, like the hospital car park.
feel: **Alarmed**, unusually for someone who always has a **plan**.
S2.quote: A coffee cart needs customers with jobs, and that's the bit I can't fix.
fieldNote: He sees the **customer side**: his side business depends on other people's wages.
Ana's **salon** is also exposed, so both incomes wobble.
His free-market view shows in blaming **fees and paperwork**.

steps.text: Keep the Northgate tills and kiosk job as long as possible
Move the coffee cart to the hospital car park and building sites
Cancel the holiday and stop meals out with Ana
Campaign to cut council pitch fees for small traders

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for people who want to work, so stop waiting for the government. Learn a skill, start something. I'd post that with a picture of the cart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think five years is decent for me. The thinking AI in 2031 hits the office jobs, but the robots don't reach Northgate till around 2034. That's time to build the cart into a proper small business with two pitches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the coffee trike in the first year, with a small loan from my uncle. I'd go to four days at Northgate and do two weekday pitches. And I'd use AI to keep the books, so I know exactly what's making money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous but good. It feels like a race I could win.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a gap between saying 'stop waiting for the government' and asking the council to cut fees?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, yes. But cutting fees isn't a handout, it's getting out of the way. I don't want the council to give me anything, I want them to stop taking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the cart failed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Go back to full-time at Northgate if they'd have me, and pay my uncle back slowly. Or try a trade, maybe plumbing, because pipes don't move themselves. I'd survive, I always have.

say: Five years is enough for people who **want to work**.
People should **learn a skill** or start something instead of **waiting**.
think: Robots don't reach Northgate till about **2034**, giving him time.
He can grow the cart into a business with **two pitches**.
do: **Buy** the **coffee trike** with a small loan from his uncle.
**Work** four days at Northgate and run **two weekday pitches**.
**Use** AI to keep the **books** and track profit.
feel: **Nervous** but good, like a **race** he could win.
S3.quote: I don't want the council to give me anything, I want them to stop taking.
fieldNote: He resolves the **fees contradiction** as removing barriers, not asking for help.
Five years makes his **business plan** feel winnable.
Still anxious: **thin savings** and a family loan mean failure would hurt.

steps.text: Buy a coffee trike with a small loan from his uncle
Run two weekday coffee pitches alongside four days at Northgate
Use an AI bookkeeping tool to track cart profit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so anyone who doesn't prepare only has themselves to blame. Harsh, maybe, but true. I'd say it on the market, with a smile.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd feel quite good. By 2039 I'll be thirty-seven and I want to own a little coffee shop in Hollybrook by then. AI can do the ordering and the books, and I'll do the coffee and the chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd keep Northgate full-time and build savings, because there's no rush. In two or three years I'd get the trike and a second pitch. By five years in, I'd look at renting a small shop unit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Excited, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'only has themselves to blame'. Would you say that to Brenda on the tills?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not Brenda, she's sixty and that's different. I mean people my age, who've got time. I'd still help Brenda fill in forms if she asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the coffee shop dream fall apart?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If nobody in my town has a job, nobody buys coffee. That's the bit I can't control. So I'd want a few things on the go, not just one.

say: Ten years is a **gift**, so people who don't prepare have themselves to **blame**.
He'd say it on the market, **with a smile**.
think: By **thirty-seven** he wants to own a small **coffee shop** in Hollybrook.
AI can do the ordering and books while he does **coffee and chat**.
do: **Keep** Northgate full-time and **build savings** this year.
**Buy** the trike and add a **second pitch** in two or three years.
**Rent** a small **shop unit** about five years in.
feel: **Calm**, and even **excited** about the decade ahead.
S4.quote: If nobody in my town has a job, nobody buys coffee.
fieldNote: He softens his blame for older workers like **Brenda**.
His long plan is a **coffee shop** run with AI help.
His remaining worry is **local wages** collapsing, which he can't control.

steps.text: Keep full-time hours at Northgate this year
Build savings before buying the coffee trike
Rent a small shop unit for a coffee shop within five years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because my customers lose their jobs before I've built anything. What would help is lower fees and less paperwork for small traders, and apprenticeships for real trades. I don't want handouts, I want a fair chance to earn.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the kiosk regulars. Old Ron buys one scratch card every morning just to have someone ask about his knee, and no machine is going to ask about his knee.

headlineQuote: I don't want handouts, I want a fair chance to earn.
portrait: Tomas, 27, works the tills, the **tobacco kiosk** and the delivery van at Northgate in Hollybrook.
He lives with Ana, a **hairdresser**, and runs a Sunday **coffee cart** planned with AI every day.
Traditional and free-market, he dislikes **handouts** and blames council fees for holding traders back.
He sees the gap before robots as time to grow the cart, but worries about **customers' wages**.
He stays **uneasy** in slower worlds and turns **alarmed** at AGI by 2028.
biggestWorry: AGI by **2028**, because his **customers** lose their jobs first.
whatWouldHelp: **Lower fees** and less paperwork for small traders.
**Apprenticeships** in real trades instead of handouts.
